title: AWS CWI Training in Columbus, OH: 6-Day Exam Prep
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for central Ohio's fab, data center, battery plant and utility welding work. Corporate, online or one-to-one formats.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Columbus, Ohio: Six Days for Central Ohio's Construction, Manufacturing and Utility Welding Inspectors
html:
Central Ohio is building at a scale few US regions can match: a semiconductor site in New Albany, data centers spreading across the suburbs, a battery plant down I-71 and the utility and highway work that has to keep up. All of it is welded, and all of it needs inspectors who can judge that welding against a code. Atlantis NDT runs a six-day (6-day) preparation course for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) examination that takes Columbus welders, fitters, QC staff and engineers through Part A Fundamentals, Part B Practical and Part C Code Application. It comes in three formats: corporate (the six days at your employer's site), online (self-paced with an instructor on hand for questions) and one-to-one (sessions with the instructor for a single candidate, online or in person). AWS administers the examination and awards the credential. Atlantis prepares people for it, certifies nobody, and has no Atlantis classroom in Columbus; its offices are in Houston, Texas and Hyderabad, India. To scope a course, send a Columbus CWI enquiry.

A welding town that runs on research as well as production

Columbus is unusual among US cities because welding is studied here as an engineering discipline, not only practised as a trade. The Ohio State University offers a Bachelor of Science in Welding Engineering, accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, that prepares students in welding materials, design, processes and nondestructive evaluation; the program marked its 75th year in 2023, and the university also offers a master's degree in welding engineering online. Also in Columbus, EWI (founded as the Edison Welding Institute in 1984 under Ohio's Thomas Edison Program) keeps its headquarters in the city. It is a nonprofit engineering and technology organization that develops and applies joining and manufacturing technology for aerospace, automotive, defense, energy and medical clients.

That research base shapes the CWI market in two ways. First, there are more welding engineers here than in most cities, and many of them sit the CWI because a client, a contract or their own employer wants a certified inspector's signature alongside the engineering judgment. Second, the eligibility arithmetic is kinder to them: AWS lists one year of welding-related experience for a bachelor's degree or higher in welding engineering or welding technology, compared with five years on a high school diploma. A welding engineering graduate with a year on a fabrication or construction job may already qualify.

How the six days fit a central Ohio schedule

The course follows one outline in every format. Days one and two cover fundamentals: welding processes and terms, joint design and welding symbols, then metallurgy, mechanical testing, discontinuities, NDT methods, safety and the arithmetic that turns up in Part A. Day three rehearses the practical. Day four is spent inside your chosen code book. Day five is timed practice papers, and day six goes back over weak spots and the logistics of the examination itself. The national AWS CWI exam prep page breaks each day down.

  • Corporate suits a contractor or manufacturer preparing several people together. The six days take place at that employer's facility, using its gauges, its weld samples and, where it fits, the code and procedures its crews already follow.
  • Online suits an individual on a construction rotation. You receive a study plan built on the six-day outline, course materials, original practice questions and timed practice papers, and you send questions to an instructor whenever they arise. Nothing happens at a fixed hour.
  • One-to-one suits a single candidate who wants direct coaching: six days of one-to-one sessions with the instructor, online or in person at a location agreed when you book.

Every practice question in the course is original Atlantis material written to the AWS topic list. None is an AWS examination question, and AWS has not approved, accredited or endorsed the course.

The central Ohio construction wave, project by project

Intel's Ohio One site in New Albany

Intel's Ohio One campus in New Albany, Licking County, has been under construction since 2022. In February 2025 Intel told its Ohio employees it would continue building at a slower pace, with the first fab's construction now planned to finish in 2030 and production to start between 2030 and 2031, and the second fab following in 2031 and 2032. Even at a slower pace a fab is a large welding job. The structure is heavy steel. The process side is miles of piping for gases, chemicals, water and exhaust, much of it stainless and much of it joined by orbital gas tungsten arc welding under tight cleanliness controls. Process piping of that kind is generally designed to ASME B31.3, with the owner's own high-purity specifications layered on top, and the inspectors who check it spend as much time on weld logs, purge records and borescope findings as on the welds themselves.

Data centers around New Albany and beyond

A report covered by Ohio public radio in January 2026 projected that Columbus will pass New York City to become the second-largest data center hub in the Great Lakes region, after Chicago. The same report counted more than 100 operational data centers in Ohio with 77 more slated by 2030, and described Meta's Prometheus facility in New Albany as the first data center to need more than a gigawatt of power. For welding inspectors, data centers mean steel buildings and equipment platforms welded to AWS D1.1, chilled-water and fuel piping in central plants, and electrical substations with their own steel. Owners build them quickly and repeat designs across sites, so a contractor that gets the inspection program right on one building tends to carry it to the next.

Honda's battery plant and the Ohio EV hub

Honda and LG Energy Solution broke ground in February 2023 on a joint-venture battery plant of more than two million square feet near Jeffersonville, at I-71 and US 35, about 40 miles southwest of Columbus. Honda's chief executive called Ohio the company's new EV hub, noting more than 40 years of Honda production and development in the state. Battery cell lines themselves involve laser and ultrasonic joining under the manufacturer's own standards rather than any CWI code book. The plant construction around them, and the conveyors, mezzanines and utility systems, is ordinary structural and piping work that a CWI inspects.

Utilities, pipelines and highway steel

Underneath the headline projects runs steadier work. Gas utilities across central Ohio replace and extend mains and stations, and steel gas lines are welded and accepted under API 1104, which federal pipeline safety rules adopt by reference. Interstate and state highway projects around the I-70 and I-71 corridors bring bridge steel fabricated to AWS D1.5. Power for the new data centers means substations, transmission structures and, at some sites, on-site generation plants with their own boiler or power piping work.

Who hires CWIs in central Ohio, and what they look for

  • General contractors and steel erectors on fab, data center and plant sites, who need shop and field weld inspection to D1.1 and records an owner's quality team will accept.
  • Mechanical contractors doing process, high-purity and central plant piping. They test candidates on Section IX and B31.3 before anything else.
  • Structural fabricators across Ohio supplying steel to those projects, many of whom want a CWI named on their quality plan.
  • Testing and inspection agencies that perform welding inspection for owners and building officials on larger buildings.
  • Manufacturers and engineering organizations, where welding engineers add the CWI so they can sign inspection records as well as design joints.
  • Owner's representatives who oversee contractors on behalf of large technology and utility clients.

What they want in common: the code book that matches their work, documented welding experience AWS will accept, and an inspector who can explain a rejection clearly to a superintendent under schedule pressure.

Choosing your Part C code for Columbus work

Part C is an open-book test on the code you pick. Choose the one that matches the work you do or want to do, because that is the book you will be reaching for every day afterwards.

Your central Ohio workBook to considerNotes
Data center, fab, battery plant and warehouse steel; structural fabricationAWS D1.1Buildings and industrial structures; prequalified joints, qualification and visual acceptance
Fab process piping, central utility plants, boiler and power pipingASME Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3Owners' high-purity specifications sit on top of B31.3 and are not themselves an exam option
Steel gas mains, stations and transmission linesAPI 1104Pipeline welder and procedure qualification and acceptance standards
ODOT and interstate bridge steelAWS D1.5Bridge fabrication, including fracture-critical members
Aerospace hardware and research work for aerospace clientsAWS D17.1Fusion welding for aerospace applications, where a customer specification calls it up

AWS names the edition it examines, which can trail the newest printing, so check your application before you start tabbing a book. Related reading: AWS D1.1, D1.1 weld acceptance criteria, API 1104 and the WPS, PQR and WPQ guide.

The AWS Columbus Section

The AWS Columbus Section belongs to AWS District 7, which its own site describes as covering more than half of Ohio along with parts of eastern Indiana, northern Kentucky, most of West Virginia and southwestern Pennsylvania. The section's boundaries take in 22 Ohio counties, and it lists about 400 individual members, 16 corporate members and seven educational institution members. It is a founding member of the Columbus Technical Societies, a cooperative of eight central Ohio technical organizations that take turns hosting monthly meetings from September through April, and it holds a business meeting in May and a golf outing in early June. The section also awards a scholarship, endowed through the AWS Foundation, to students within its boundaries who are focused on welding or welding engineering.

For a CWI candidate, those meetings are a good place to find people who will verify your welding history for the AWS application, to hear which contractors are hiring inspectors for the big projects, and to meet engineers from the university and from industry who sit on the other side of the inspection report.

From welding student, tradesperson or engineer to CWI

Columbus candidates arrive by three main routes, and each meets the AWS rules differently.

  • Welding engineering graduates. A bachelor's degree in welding engineering puts you in the one-year experience row. The work still has to be welding-related and verifiable, so a year in a research lab may not count the way a year on a production floor or construction site does; AWS decides.
  • Tradespeople. Pipefitters, ironworkers, boilermakers and production welders usually come in on the high school row (five years) or the trade-course row (four years). Their difficulty is rarely the welding; it is the paperwork trail for experience spread across contractors and sites.
  • QC and NDT technicians. People already inspecting under someone else's signature know the job and need the theory, symbols and code navigation the examination tests.

Whatever the route, gather your records early: dates, employers, sites, the codes you worked to and a contact who can confirm each job.

Booking the examination from central Ohio

AWS reviews your application and sends a confirmation letter carrying an eligibility code. With that code you reserve Part A and Part C at a Prometric test center; AWS says Prometric has more than 450 centers worldwide and over 100 in the United States, and its site shows those closest to Columbus. Part B is handled separately, at the seminar and examination locations where AWS itself runs the practical, which can mean a trip. Look up the current AWS seminar and exam schedule first, pick a practical date you can reach, then book the computer-based parts within the order and window AWS sets.

Part A asks 150 questions on fundamentals. Part B combines hands-on tasks using AWS-supplied tools and specimens with 46 questions. Part C puts roughly 50 to 65 questions to you with your code book open. AWS requires at least 72 percent on each part and publishes its examination fees on aws.org. The CWI exam budget planner helps you add up travel, books and time away from work.

Studying around construction schedules

Construction in central Ohio runs in phases, and inspectors on a big site often work long weeks while steel or piping is going in and then have quieter spells between packages. Plan the six days around that rhythm.

  1. Use a quiet spell for the two fundamentals blocks; they are the most reading-heavy part of the course.
  2. During busy weeks, keep the code book with you and look up the provisions behind the joints you inspect. Ten minutes a day inside D1.1 or B31.3 builds the navigation speed Part C rewards.
  3. Practise practical measurements on real welds with real gauges, and write the numbers down before you judge them.
  4. Save the timed practice papers for the final weeks before your Prometric date, and let the scores decide where your last study hours go.

Corporate: six days at a central Ohio contractor or plant

For an employer, the corporate format brings the full six days to its own site for a group of its people. A mechanical contractor might prepare its piping inspectors for B31.3 work on a fab job; a structural fabricator might want several CWIs before a data center package starts; a manufacturer might prepare engineers and QC leads together. The practical day uses the company's own fillet, bridge cam and hi-lo gauges on welds from its own work, and the code day can split by book when a group is heading for different codes. Dates can be fitted around project phases. Each person still applies to AWS individually and must meet the experience and vision requirements in their own right.

One-to-one: online or face to face

One-to-one preparation gives a single candidate six days of sessions with the instructor, online or in person at a location agreed when booking. It works well for a welding engineer who knows metallurgy thoroughly but has never had to find a table in a code book against the clock, for an inspector whose employer needs a CWI by a fixed date, and for someone retaking one part who wants every hour aimed at it. The content is the same outline the other formats use; only the pace and focus change.

Eligibility and the vision record

Experience requirements scale with education: one year for a bachelor's or higher in welding engineering or welding technology, two for an associate degree or higher in engineering technology, engineering or physical science, four for completed trade or vocational courses and five for a high school diploma, with longer periods for less schooling. AWS also wants a visual acuity record on its form showing near vision of Jaeger J2 at 12 inches or more (glasses allowed) and a color perception test, signed by a qualified practitioner and recent enough under AWS rules on your examination date. Candidates without enough experience yet can consider the Certified Associate Welding Inspector. The complete table is on the AWS CWI exam prep course page; for a wider view of requirements and careers, read CWI requirements and career impact.

After the CWI in Columbus

A CWI stays valid for nine years under AWS rules, with renewals at years three and six. In a market this varied, the next step depends on where you work.

  • Senior CWI for inspectors who end up running quality programs on large projects; see the SCWI pathway.
  • Endorsements for inspectors who move between structural, piping and pipeline work and want recognition on more than one book.
  • NDT certification for those who want to run ultrasonic or penetrant tests themselves. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the employer certifies after training and logged method experience; Atlantis provides that training. See NDT training in Columbus, VT Level 2, UT Level 2 and PT Level 2.

To weigh the credentials, see the AWS CWI, API 577 and ASNT Level II comparison; Atlantis offers API exam prep separately, as self-paced online courses. For inspection work in the region, see ultrasonic testing in Columbus and inspection services in Ohio. The Practical NDT welding workshop lets you rehearse inspection steps in a browser between sessions.

Other Ohio Valley CWI pages, and a Columbus quote

Nearby CWI exam prep pages: Cleveland, Cincinnati, Pittsburgh, Louisville, Indianapolis and Detroit. For how results differ by part, read CWI results by exam part.

For a quote, tell us the format you want, how many candidates there are, each person's schooling and welding experience in outline, and the Part C book each intends to choose. For corporate delivery, add the site location, the gauges and weld samples available, and any project phases to work around. Request a Columbus CWI exam prep quote; pricing is given on request.

faq.q: Does Atlantis run CWI classes in a Columbus classroom?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Columbus. The six-day course is delivered online at your own pace, as one-to-one sessions with the instructor (online or in person at an agreed location), or as a corporate course at your employer's site. See the outline.

faq.q: I have an Ohio State welding engineering degree. How much experience do I need?
faq.a: AWS lists one year of welding-related work experience for a bachelor's degree or higher in welding engineering or welding technology. The experience must be verifiable and welding-related, and AWS decides what counts, so describe your work carefully on the application.

The American Welding Society. It reviews eligibility, runs every part of the examination and issues the CWI. Atlantis prepares candidates and certifies no one; AWS has not endorsed or approved the course.

faq.q: Which Part C code suits data center and fab structural steel?
faq.a: AWS D1.1, the structural steel code used for buildings and industrial structures. See AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Which code fits process piping on a semiconductor site?
faq.a: The ASME option, which covers Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3. Fab process piping is generally designed to B31.3, with the owner's high-purity specifications added on top; those specifications are not an examination option.

faq.q: Where do Columbus candidates sit the exam?
faq.a: Fundamentals and Code Application are computer-based and booked at a Prometric center with the eligibility code from your AWS confirmation letter. The practical runs only at AWS seminar and examination locations, so check the AWS schedule and be ready to travel.

faq.q: Can a data center contractor have the course delivered on site?
faq.a: Yes. The corporate format runs all six days at your facility for a group of your staff, using your own gauges and welds and splitting the code day by book if needed. Request a quote.

faq.q: Can I do the one-to-one format in person in Columbus?
faq.a: Yes, at a location agreed when you book, or online if you prefer. You get six days of one-to-one sessions with the instructor following the same outline as the other formats.

faq.q: Are any practice questions real AWS questions?
faq.a: No. All practice questions and timed papers are original material written by Atlantis against the published AWS topic areas.

faq.q: Should a Columbus CWI also learn NDT?
faq.a: Many do, especially on large construction sites where an inspector who can also run UT or PT is valuable. Atlantis provides ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based training and the employer certifies afterwards; see NDT training in Columbus.
